Platform audio research: iOS, Android, macOS

The product lives or dies on one question: can the DJ hear something different from the crowd? This document records what each platform can actually do, what needs extra hardware, and what needs platform-specific code. It drove every decision in ../architecture.md.

Legend: ✅ works with the device alone · 🔌 needs external hardware · ⚙️ needs platform-specific code · ❌ not possible

1. The core problem, stated precisely

A DJ needs two independent audio buses:

BusWho hears itContents
MasterThe roomThe mix
Cue (headphones / PFL)Only the DJThe next track, previewed and beat-matched before it is audible, optionally blended with the master

A phone has, at most, one stereo output that the OS will give an app by default. Everything below is about getting a second independent stereo (or mono) path, and about being honest when there isn't one.

The system volume buttons are not a mixer: they scale the whole hardware output, so in any shared- output configuration (e.g. a splitter cable) they move master and cue together. The engine therefore owns independent master gain, headphone gain, cue/master blend and per-channel gain, and treats the hardware volume as a fixed calibration that the user sets once.

2. iOS / iPadOS

Routing model

  • AVAudioSession category .playback sends audio to the last-connected output only: one route.
  • Category .multiRoute routes distinct streams to different outputs at the same time — Apple's own example is a USB device plus headphones — and requires observing route-change notifications because a route change can invalidate the configuration.
  • Apple documents the valid multi-route combinations as USB + headphones, HDMI + headphones, Line-out + headphones. The OS presents them as one aggregate device; currentRoute tells you which channels of the aggregate belong to which port. Long-standing Core Audio guidance is that multi-route needs something in the headphone port and does not work with AirPlay or Bluetooth.
  • A class-compliant USB interface or DJ controller with ≥ 4 outputs appears as a single multichannel port; setPreferredOutputNumberOfChannels unlocks all channels.

What that means

ScenarioiOSNotes
Master on built-in speaker, cue in AirPods❌Speaker and Bluetooth can't be used together by one app
Master on Bluetooth speaker, cue in wired headphones❌Bluetooth is excluded from multi-route
One wired output + stereo→mono splitter cable🔌 ⚙️L = master (mono), R = cue (mono). The established mobile technique (djay "Split Output")
USB-C DAC/interface for master + wired headphones🔌 ⚙️.multiRoute, channel map from currentRoute
4-channel USB interface / DJ controller🔌Single device, single clock — the best experience
HDMI / Line-out for master + headphones🔌 ⚙️Multi-route
Bluetooth master, no cue✅Works; latency must be compensated in the UI (playhead, waveform)

Open question to verify on device (Routing Lab): how the USB-C-to-3.5 mm adapter on USB-C iPhones is classified (.headphones vs .usbAudio) and whether it combines with a second USB DAC through a hub under .multiRoute.

Latency

  • setPreferredIOBufferDuration(0.005) typically yields 128–256 frames at 48 kHz on modern devices.
  • outputLatency + ioBufferDuration gives the figure used for alignment and for drawing the playhead.

3. Android

Low-latency stack

  • Oboe (Apache-2.0, C++) wraps AAudio on Android 8.1+ and OpenSL ES below.
  • Google's checklist: request PerformanceMode::LowLatency, request Exclusive sharing (MMAP — writes straight into the buffer the DSP reads), use a data callback, and don't block in it. Google's own measurements (round-trip): ~20 ms with all recommendations; 205 ms without low-latency mode; 160 ms when an app requests 44.1 kHz on AAudio (system resampling path) vs 23 ms with Oboe's resampler — so the engine runs at the device's native rate.
  • Exclusive mode may be refused or later revoked; the stream must be inspected after opening.

Device selection and multichannel

  • AudioManager.getDevices(GET_DEVICES_OUTPUTS) lists outputs with type, channel counts and channel index masks. setDeviceId() binds a stream to a device and is honoured on AAudio (API 28+) but not on OpenSL ES → minSdk 28.
  • Channel index masks address USB channels by number (a 4-channel interface is 0xF; master on 0/1, cue on 2/3) rather than by speaker position. AAudio opens > 2-channel streams with an index mask, so channel n of the stream is physical output n.

Two outputs at once

  • Android 12 added combined audio device routing — but through system APIs for privileged apps (setPreferredDevicesForStrategy), not for third-party apps. The same page notes simultaneous routing to multiple USB devices isn't supported; Android 14 relaxes this for USB devices of different types given kernel/vendor support.
  • For a normal app, opening a second stream on a different device is policy-dependent per phone: the OS may silently re-route it. The host therefore treats a second device as a capability to probe: open, compare getDeviceId() with the request, fall back to master-only (and tell the user) if it was re-routed.
ScenarioAndroidNotes
4-channel USB interface / DJ controller🔌Best path; one stream, index-mask channels
USB-C splitter / headphone dongle + splitter cable🔌 ⚙️Split-mono
Speaker (master) + wired headphones (cue)⚙️ probeWorks on some devices; many force media to the headset
USB DAC (master) + wired headset (cue)⚙️ probeDifferent device types; vendor-dependent
Bluetooth master✅Latency compensation needed

4. macOS

  • Core Audio exposes every device; an app can run any number of output devices concurrently, each on its own clock. Enumeration: kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices, stream configuration (channels), transport type, latency + safety offset + buffer size.
  • Aggregate devices (Audio MIDI Setup, or programmatically via AudioHardwareCreateAggregateDevice) combine devices into one; drift compensation is enabled per sub-device (kAudioSubDevicePropertyDriftCompensation), with a quality setting from 0–128. Historically the HAL's compensation was a simple sample doubling/dropping algorithm.
  • Decision: prefer one multichannel device; otherwise run the cue bus on a second device through the engine's own drift-compensated resampler (cubic Hermite + PI-controlled ratio). This avoids asking users to build aggregate devices and gives better quality than sample dropping. Measured in tests: < 20 ppm ratio wander (≈ 0.03 cent), zero underruns across ±500 ppm drift with mismatched buffer sizes.
ScenariomacOS
Built-in speakers (master) + headphone jack (cue)⚙️ two devices, drift-compensated
USB interface ≥ 4 ch🔌 single device
Bluetooth speaker master + wired headphones cue⚙️ + cue delayed to line up with the speaker
DJ controller with audio🔌

5. Bluetooth

Codec / pathTypical added latencyUsable for
SBC / AAC (A2DP)100–200 msMaster playback with compensation; not cueing
LE Audio / LC3 (Android 13+ where supported)tens of msBorderline for cueing; still not recommended
aptX Low Latency / LC3pluslower, hardware-specificRare on phones

iOS does not expose the active codec. Neither platform lets an app choose it.

Policy:

  1. Never deny Bluetooth — beginners will use it for master.
  2. Read the OS-reported latency and shift the waveform/playhead so what you see matches what the room hears.
  3. When master is wireless and cue is wired, delay the cue bus by the difference so beat-matching by ear still works (sbe_engine_set_latency_compensation).
  4. Never delay the master to wait for slow headphones; report it instead.
  5. AirPlay/Cast buffer for seconds: playback only.

6. Engine options evaluated

OptionVerdict
AVAudioEngine (Apple) / AAudio directly (Android)Good hosts, but two separate mixers to keep identical — rejected as the engine; used as the host layer
JUCEMature, cross-platform; GPL or commercial licence, large footprint, owns the app structure — rejected
SuperpoweredDJ-focused and fast; commercial licence fees per platform, closed source — kept as fallback for time-stretch only
miniaudioExcellent portable I/O; no DJ-specific routing control on mobile — not needed given native hosts
Own C++17 core + thin native hosts✅ Chosen. One mixer, one set of tests, identical behaviour on every platform; hosts are ~300 lines each

Supporting libraries planned (licence-checked):

  • Time-stretch / key-lock: Signalsmith Stretch (MIT) first; Rubber Band (GPL/commercial) as benchmark.
  • Tempo sync with other apps/devices: Ableton Link SDK (GPLv2 or proprietary licence from Ableton).
  • Stems: on-device source separation via Core ML / Android NNAPI-backed runtimes (Phase 3).

7. Music sources (a constraint the brief doesn't mention)

DRM-protected streaming catalogues cannot be decoded from files; they require licensed partner integrations:

  • Spotify withdrew DJ-app support in 2020 and returned in September 2025 to the desktop versions of rekordbox, Serato and djay only — mobile versions excluded.
  • Apple Music opened DJ integration to rekordbox, Serato, Engine DJ and others in March 2025 (djay since 2024).
  • TIDAL has been available in the major DJ apps for some time.

Implication: launch on local files (Files app / MediaStore / Finder, plus Apple Music library items that are DRM-free), design the library layer for pluggable providers, and pursue partner agreements early — they gate the beginner audience more than any feature.
